blocks.text: Geometry questions here are **angle-chasing**: each figure hides a chain of small, certain facts—vertical angles, straight lines, triangle sums—and you follow the chain link by link until the unknown falls out. The full toolkit is short:

rows: angles on a line sum to $180°$
angles around a point sum to $360°$
opposite angles at a crossing are **equal**
only **two** angle values exist, summing to $180°$
equals the **sum of the two remote interior** angles

items: **Mark everything you deduce on the figure**—each new angle unlocks the next.
**At any crossing:** vertical angles match; neighbors sum to $180°$.
**Parallel lines:** decide equal (both acute or both obtuse) vs. supplementary (one of each)—that's the whole classification.
**In triangles:** two known angles always buy the third; tick marks (equal sides) buy equal angles.
**Similar triangles:** match corresponding sides *by position across from equal angles*, then set up one proportion—in the same order on both sides.

blocks.text: Figures on the SAT are usually to scale unless marked otherwise—use your eyes to *check* (an angle that looks acute isn't $130°$), but use the chain of facts to *prove*.

blocks.caption: Two lines crossing: four angles, two facts.
blocks.alt: Two crossing lines forming an X, with the left angle marked 130 degrees, the right angle marked x, and the top angle marked y

items.note: **Linear pair** — neighbors on a straight line sum to $180°$

blocks.text: Around a full point, the angles complete a circle: they sum to $\blue{360°}$. Keep the two totals straight—**line $180°$, point $360°$**—because the test builds traps from exactly that mix-up:

blocks.stem: Three angles measuring $x°$, $2x°$, and $60°$ together form a complete rotation **around a point**. What is the value of $x$?

items.text: Around a point: $x + 2x + 60 = 360$, so $3x = 300$ and $x = 100$.
$40$ solves $3x + 60 = 180$—the **straight line** total, but these angles complete a full rotation.
$60$ just copies the given angle; nothing forces $x$ to match it.
$200$ is $2x$—the middle angle's measure, not $x$.

blocks.text: Angle-chasing bookkeeping: every time you compute an angle, write it on the figure immediately. The next fact is usually waiting right next to it.

A transversal crossing **parallel** lines creates eight angles—but only **two different values**. Every acute angle equals every other acute; every obtuse equals every obtuse; and any acute–obtuse pair sums to $180°$.

blocks.caption: $\ell \parallel m$. The $65°$ angle sits at the top crossing; $a°$ and $b°$ at the bottom one.
blocks.alt: Two parallel horizontal lines cut by a transversal, with 65 degrees marked at the top intersection and angles a and b at the bottom intersection

items.note: Alternate interior angles (the “Z” pattern) — both acute, so **equal**
Same-side interior angles — one acute, one obtuse, so **supplementary**

blocks.text: Skip the vocabulary quiz (corresponding, alternate, co-interior…) and ask one question: **do the two angles look the same type, or different?** Same type → equal. Different → sum to $180°$. That shortcut answers every parallel-line question—when the lines are parallel.

blocks.caption: The two marked angles are alternate interior angles.
blocks.alt: Parallel lines with a transversal; 105 degrees marked at the top intersection and the expression 2x plus 25 degrees at the bottom intersection

blocks.stem: In the figure, lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel. What is the value of $x$?

items.text: Both angles are the same type (the “Z” pair), so they're equal: $2x + 25 = 105$, giving $2x = 80$ and $x = 40$.
$x = 25$ comes from $2x + 25 = 75$—treating the pair as supplementary. They're the same type, so they match, not sum.
$x = 52.5$ halves the $105$ without ever subtracting the $25$.
$x = 105$ confuses the *angle's* measure with $x$—the variable inside the expression.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: The interior angles of **every** triangle sum to $180°$. Two known angles always determine the third.

blocks.alt: A triangle with angles 52 degrees, 63 degrees, and x degrees

blocks.text: Extend one side and the new **exterior angle** equals the sum of the two **remote** interior angles—the triangle sum and the straight line, fused into one step:

blocks.caption: The $115°$ exterior angle gathers the two remote interior angles.
blocks.alt: A triangle with one side extended, forming an exterior angle of 115 degrees; the remote interior angles are 45 degrees and x degrees

items.note: Exterior $=$ sum of the two **remote** interiors
One subtraction — no need to find the third angle first

blocks.text: Equal sides (shown by tick marks) sit opposite **equal angles**. Given the apex angle, the two base angles split what's left of $180°$ evenly.

blocks.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = AC$ and the measure of angle $A$ is $48°$. What is the measure of angle $B$?

items.text: The equal sides $AB$ and $AC$ face equal angles at $B$ and $C$: each is $\frac{180 - 48}{2} = 66°$.
$48°$ copies angle $A$—but $A$ is the *apex* between the equal sides, not one of the matched pair.
$132°$ is $180 - 48$ **unhalved**—the two base angles' combined share, not one angle.
$42°$ computes $90 - 48$: a complement, which nothing in this triangle asks for.

blocks.text: {blue|Similar} triangles are the same shape at different sizes: **all angles equal, all sides scaled by the same factor**. Two matching angles are enough to prove it (AA)—the third comes free from the triangle sum.

blocks.caption: Same shape, scale factor $\frac{9}{6} = 1.5$: every side of the large triangle is $1.5$ times its partner.
blocks.alt: A small triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 next to a similar larger triangle with sides 9, 12, 15

items.note: Scale factor from one **matched pair** of sides
Every other side scales by the same $k$

blocks.text: The SAT's favorite similar-triangle setup hides one triangle inside another: a segment drawn **parallel to a side** creates a smaller triangle similar to the whole thing.

blocks.caption: $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$, so $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$.
blocks.alt: Triangle ABC with segment DE drawn parallel to base BC; AD is 4, DB is 2, DE is 6, and BC is x

items.note: The big triangle's side is the **whole** length $AD + DB$
Corresponding sides, same order: small over big

blocks.text: The classic nested-triangle error: using $DB = 2$ in the ratio. The big triangle's side runs from $A$ all the way to $B$—compare **whole side to whole side** ($AD$ with $AB$), never the leftover piece.

blocks.stem: A person $6$ feet tall casts a shadow $4$ feet long. At the same time, a nearby tree casts a shadow $18$ feet long. What is the height, in feet, of the tree?

items.text: Sunlight makes two similar right triangles: $\frac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}} = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5$ for both, so the tree is $18 \times 1.5 = 27$ feet.
$12$ uses the ratio upside down ($18 \times \frac{4}{6}$)—that would make the tree *shorter* relative to its shadow than the person.
$16$ reasons additively (“the person's height is $2$ more than the shadow”)—similarity scales by multiplication, never by a fixed difference.
$72$ multiplies $18 \times 4$—two lengths multiplied gives an area-like number, not a height.

blocks.text: Chase the chain: mark what you know, apply one fact at a time—and in similarity questions, check the ratio's order twice.

blocks.stem: Two lines intersect, and a pair of **vertical** angles measures $(3x - 10)°$ and $(2x + 15)°$. What is the value of $x$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Vertical angles are equal:

items.text: $35$ solves $5x + 5 = 180$—treating the pair as a **linear pair**. Vertical angles match; neighbors sum.
$5$ comes from botching the collection step ($x = 15 - 10$).
$65$ is each angle's **measure**—the question asks for $x$.

blocks.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two **same-side interior** angles measure $(5x)°$ and $(4x)°$. What is the value of $x$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Same-side interior angles are one acute, one obtuse—**supplementary**:

items.text: $36$ sets $5x = 180$ alone—as if one angle filled the whole straight line.
$45$ does the same with $4x = 180$.
$10$ solves $9x = 90$—a right angle where the fact demands $180°$.

blocks.alt: A triangle with one side extended forming an exterior angle of 126 degrees; the remote interior angles are 58 degrees and x degrees

blocks.stem: In the figure, what is the value of $x$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Exterior angle theorem: $x + 58 = 126$, so $x = 68$.

items.text: Check the long way: the interior angle beside $126°$ is $54°$, and $68 + 58 + 54 = 180$. {green|✓}
$54$ is $180 - 126$: the *adjacent* interior angle, not the remote $x$.
$32$ computes $90 - 58$—no right angle appears anywhere in this figure.
$63$ halves the $126$, as if the two remote angles had to be equal. Nothing says they are.

blocks.stem: In triangle $ABC$, point $D$ lies on side $\overline{AB}$ and point $E$ lies on side $\overline{AC}$ such that $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$. If $AD = 6$, $AB = 9$, and $DE = 10$, what is the length of $\overline{BC}$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ because $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$:

items.note: Small triangle to big triangle — whole sides, both times
Same ratio for every pair of corresponding sides

items.text: The big triangle is $\frac{3}{2}$ the size, so its base is $15$. {green|✓}
$6.7 \approx 10 \times \frac{6}{9}$ shrinks instead of enlarging—$BC$ belongs to the *bigger* triangle.
$13$ adds the difference $9 - 6 = 3$ to $10$—additive thinking where similarity multiplies.
$30$ scales by $DB = 3$ as a *factor*—the leftover piece $DB$ isn't a side of either similar triangle.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: Line $= 180°$, point $= 360°$, vertical angles equal. Write every deduced angle on the figure.
Parallel lines + transversal: only two values exist—same type → **equal**, different type → **supplementary**.
Triangle sum $180°$; the exterior angle equals the sum of the two **remote** interiors—one step instead of two.
Isosceles: equal sides face equal angles; base angles $= \frac{180 - \text{apex}}{2}$.
Similar triangles (AA): sides scale by one factor $k$. Set ratios in **matching order**, and in nested figures compare **whole side to whole side**—never the leftover piece.
Similarity multiplies, never adds—an answer built from a *difference* of sides is a trap.
